# PROTOCOL.md — the course state machine

Five rounds. Every round runs four phases, in order:

```
TUTOR  →  SPEC  →  BUILD  →  DEMO
```

- **TUTOR** — Socratic Q&A from `round-N/questions.md`; the learner's accepted answers
  are recorded into `round-N/answers.md` as they go. Ends when the gate passes.
- **SPEC** — recorded answers become clauses in `spec/spec.md` (learner confirms
  wording). Produces a spec diff.
- **BUILD** — the agent patches `src/snackbot.py` toward `round-N/reference/`, scoped by
  `round-N/build.md`, until `round-N/verify.sh` passes. Produces a code diff.
- **DEMO** — the learner operates the app per `round-N/demo.md`: predict → run →
  observe → record. Produces an entry in `course/demo-log.md`.

Modes, mode tags (`[R2 · TUTOR]`), and the EXPAND sub-mode are defined in AGENTS.md.

## Git is the state machine

No state file. Each phase ends in exactly one commit, carrying exactly one artifact:

| phase ends | commit name | contains |
|---|---|---|
| TUTOR (gate passes) | `round-N tutor` | `course/rounds/round-N/answers.md` |
| SPEC | `round-N spec` | `spec/spec.md` |
| BUILD | `round-N build` | `src/snackbot.py` |
| DEMO | `round-N demo` | `course/demo-log.md` |

Because commits carry different artifacts, **diffs shown to the learner are always
scoped** — each phase file states its exact command (`git diff HEAD~1 -- spec/`,
`git diff HEAD~1 -- src/`).

## Resume table

Derive position from the **last course commit** in `git log --oneline`, then check
`git status --porcelain`. A *course commit* is one named `round-N tutor|spec|build|demo`.
Any other commit in the log — the repo's own history — is not course state; **if there is
no course commit at all, the course has not started.**

| last course commit | working tree | you are at |
|---|---|---|
| none | `round-1/answers.md` modified | Round 1, TUTOR — resume at first unanswered question |
| none | clean | Round 1, TUTOR — first question |
| `round-(N-1) demo` | `round-N/answers.md` modified | Round N, TUTOR — resume at first unanswered question |
| `round-(N-1) demo` | clean | Round N, TUTOR — first question |
| `round-N tutor` | — | Round N, SPEC |
| `round-N spec` | — | Round N, BUILD |
| `round-N build` | — | Round N, DEMO |
| `round-5 demo` | — | DONE — offer the wrap-up in `round-5/demo.md` |

`answers.md` stays uncommitted during TUTOR on purpose: the dirty file is the mid-round
resume signal, and it is the learner's own record — not agent bookkeeping.

## Question types and groups

Every question carries `type: single-answer` or `type: judgment` (acceptance rules in
AGENTS.md). A **question group** is several sub-questions (`Q5.1`–`Q5.6`) sharing one
output artifact and one gate: ask one at a time, produce the artifact once. Round 5 is
an ordinary round containing one group of six judgment questions — no special protocol.

## Reconciliation rule

If the working tree disagrees with the last commit (the learner edited files outside
the loop): **git history is truth for position; the round's `reference/` is truth for
what `src/` should contain at each boundary.** Ask one question — "keep your changes or
restore the round state?" — then commit theirs as `round-N learner-edit` or restore.
Never silently discard learner work; never let untracked drift into a build diff.

## The honor system, stated once

Verify scripts check the build; nothing stops a learner from reading `tutor-notes.md`,
editing `answers.md` after a reveal, or skipping phases. By design — the course
optimizes for learning, not proctoring.

`[R1 · EXPAND]`

**1. What the three tables actually hold**

Your `memory.db` has three tables:

- **`CONVERSATIONAL_MEMORY` — 5 rows.** The literal transcript: `thread_id`, `role` (user/assistant), `content`, timestamp. This is history in order, exactly as it was said. That's the five lines `show_memory.py` printed.

- **`CONVERSATION_VECTORS` — 5 rows.** The *same* five turns, stored a second way. Each row is `content` plus an `embedding`: a list of 1536 floating-point numbers. An embedding is what an embedding model produces when you hand it a piece of text — a point in 1536-dimensional space, positioned so that text with similar *meaning* lands nearby. `"I'm allergic to peanuts"` and `"avoid nuts for me"` sit close together even though they share almost no words.

  Why store the same turns twice? Because the two shapes answer different questions. The transcript table answers "what were the last N turns?" — ordered, exact, cheap. The vector table answers "which past turn is *relevant to what the user just said*?" — you embed the new message, compare it against all stored embeddings, and take the nearest ones. That comparison is why it's called semantic *search* rather than keyword search.

- **`SEMANTIC_MEMORY` — 7 rows.** Not conversation at all — standalone facts about the world, also embedded so they can be searched the same way. Here they are in full:

  1. Trail mix almost always contains peanuts and other nuts.
  2. Peanut butter energy balls are made from oats, honey and peanut butter. They contain peanuts.
  3. Sunflower seed butter is the usual substitute for people who must avoid peanuts.
  4. Edamame is steamed young soybeans: high in protein, naturally peanut-free.
  5. Rice crackers (senbei) are a common Taiwanese snack; check labels, as some are coated…
  6. Pineapple cake is a Taiwanese specialty of pineapple jam in buttery pastry…
  7. A severe peanut allergy can cause anaphylaxis. Strict avoidance is the only reliable…

  Notice this is a curated little knowledge base aimed squarely at the scenario: which snacks hide peanuts, what to substitute, what's safe, and what's local to Taipei. The "seven semantic rows" are those seven facts.

So the phrase "the allergy is stored in two forms": it's in `CONVERSATIONAL_MEMORY`/`CONVERSATION_VECTORS` as something *the user said*, and in `SEMANTIC_MEMORY` as a *fact about the world* (row 7 — anaphylaxis, strict avoidance).

**2. What `run_turn` does, line by line**

```python
def run_turn(user_msg: str) -> str:
```
Defines a function taking one string, `user_msg`, and returning a string. The `: str` and `-> str` are type hints — documentation for humans and editors; Python doesn't enforce them at runtime.

```python
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},

`[R1 · EXPAND]`

Good — `tiktoken` knows this model, so you're on `o200k_base`, its real tokenizer. No fallback.

**The two ways to know how many tokens you used**

*Way one — ask the API afterwards.* Every response object comes back with a `usage` field:

```python
response.usage.prompt_tokens      # what the provider actually billed for input
response.usage.completion_tokens  # what it actually billed for output
```

This is ground truth. It's what appears on your invoice. But it only exists **after** the call has completed and the money is spent.

*Way two — count the text yourself.* That's what `meter.py` does. `tiktoken` is the same tokenizer OpenAI's models use; you hand it a string, it hands back the list of token IDs, you take the length. No network, no cost, no API key needed.

**Why this course picked way two**

Look at where you're headed. Rounds 2–5 are all variations on one question: *how much stuff do I stuff into the prompt?* Deterministic memory says "inject the last N turns and the top-K semantic hits, every single turn." That makes the prompt bigger, and bigger prompts cost more. The entire trade-off you're being asked to reason about lives in the input token count.

Now suppose you want to ask: *"What would it cost if I injected all 5 conversation turns plus 7 semantic facts on every turn?"* With `response.usage`, the only way to find out is to make the call and pay. With local counting, you can build the prompt string, count it, price it, and decide — without sending anything. That's what "compute the cost before you spend it" means. It turns cost from a thing you observe into a thing you can *design against*.

There's a second reason. Not every LLM-adjacent operation returns a `usage` field you care about, and you may want to meter text that never becomes a request at all — a memory row you're deciding whether to include, a retrieved chunk you're deciding whether to trim. A local counter works on any string. `response.usage` only works on completed requests.

**What you give up — and it's real**

Local counting is an *estimate*, and it under-reports in three specific ways:

1. **Message overhead.** The API doesn't send your text raw; it wraps each message with role markers and separators. Those are a handful of tokens per message. `meter.py` joins the contents with `"\n"` and counts that, so it misses the wrapper — a few tokens per call, more as your message list grows.

2. **Reasoning tokens.** On reasoning-capable models, the provider may bill output tokens the model generated while thinking that never appear in `.content`. Your meter counts the visible reply only. If those exist, the real output count can exceed yours substantially.

3. **Prompt caching.** If a provider serves part of your prompt from cache at a discount, your local count says you paid full price. Your estimate is high, the invoice is lower.

And the price table itself: `PRICE_PER_1K` in `meter.py` is a hardcoded literal with a comment above it that says *"Prices drift. Check your provider's pricing page before trusting the dollars."* That's honest — those numbers are correct on the day someone typed them and not necessarily today.

**So which should you trust?**

For *comparing designs* — the entire purpose of this course — local counting is not just adequate, it's better: it's consistent, free, and available before you commit. If Round 1 costs you 40 input tokens and Round 2 costs 400, that 10× is real regardless of a few tokens of message overhead in either number.

For *predicting a bill*, use `response.usage`. Estimates are for decisions; usage is for accounting.

If you want, when you run the demo in a moment I can print both side by side — your meter's estimate and the API's actual `usage` — so you can see the size of the gap on a real call rather than take my word for it. Say the word, or say **done** and we go straight to DEMO.

`[R2 · EXPAND]`

Two decisions are hiding in that phrase, and the table shows why each one matters.

**Half one: "keyed by thread id" — whose turns?**

Every row carries `thread_id = snackbot-demo`. Right now that's the only thread, so it looks like decoration. It isn't. `CONVERSATIONAL_MEMORY` is one flat table with an autoincrementing id — it's not "the conversation," it's *every* conversation, stacked. The moment there's a second user, or the same user starts a second chat, their turns land in the same table interleaved with these.

A read written as `SELECT content FROM CONVERSATIONAL_MEMORY ORDER BY id` would fetch all of it. That's not a bug that crashes — it's a bug that pastes a stranger's conversation into your prompt and bills you for the tokens. The clause pins the read to one thread, so "the prior turns" means *this* conversation's prior turns.

It's also the scoping decision that decides what "memory" even means for your product. Per-thread means the bot forgets your allergy when you start a new chat. Per-user across all threads means it remembers — and also means one thread can contaminate another. That's a real product choice, and the clause makes it explicit rather than accidental.

**Half two: "in the order they were written" — and look at the `ts` column.**

All five timestamps read `2026-08-18 11:01:28`. Identical, to the second. The seed script wrote them in one burst, and SQLite's `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` has one-second resolution.

So `ORDER BY ts` gives SQLite five rows it considers equally ranked, and it may return them in any order it likes. You'd get a conversation like:

```
assistant: Understood. I'll avoid peanuts and anything containing them.
user:      Hi! Any snack ideas for this afternoon?
user:      Yes, important: I'm allergic to peanuts...
```

The assistant agreeing to something before it was asked. Every individual row is true; the sequence is nonsense.

`ORDER BY id` is reliable here because `id` is `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` — strictly increasing, one per insert, never tied. Insertion order *is* write order. That's why the clause says "in the order they were written" rather than "chronologically": those sound like synonyms and aren't.

**Why ordering matters beyond looking tidy**

- **Referents break.** "Understood. I'll avoid peanuts" is a reply. Detached from what it replies to, it's a floating assertion.
- **Corrections invert.** Suppose a later turn said "actually, it was a mild sensitivity, I was overstating." Order is the only thing encoding which statement supersedes which. Shuffle it and the model may act on the retracted version.
- **Recency signals get destroyed.** Models weight the end of a prompt heavily. Order determines what lands there.

And notice the through-line to Q1: every one of these decisions — which thread, what order — is made *by code, in advance, identically on every turn*. Nobody asks the model "which rows do you think you need?" That's the whole content of the word deterministic: the answers are baked into a `WHERE` clause and an `ORDER BY`, written once, and they never vary.

`[R2 · EXPAND]`

The `?` is a **parameter placeholder**. You write the SQL with a hole in it, and pass the value separately:

```python
conn.execute("... WHERE thread_id = ? ORDER BY id", (THREAD_ID,))
```

Two arguments: the SQL string, and a tuple of values to fill the holes, left to right. One `?` → one-element tuple. The INSERT has three `?` and gets a three-element tuple in matching order.

The tempting alternative is string formatting:

```python
conn.execute(f"... WHERE thread_id = '{THREAD_ID}' ORDER BY id")   # don't
```

That builds one finished string and hands it to the database. It works — right up until the value contains a quote.

**Why it breaks.** Suppose a thread id were `o'brien`. The f-string produces:

```sql
WHERE thread_id = 'o'brien'
```

The quote closes the string early, `brien'` is now stray syntax, and the query fails. That's the benign case.

**The malicious case.** Now suppose a value comes from a user, and they submit:

```
x' OR '1'='1
```

The f-string produces:

```sql
WHERE thread_id = 'x' OR '1'='1'
```

`'1'='1'` is always true, so the WHERE matches every row — every thread, every user. Your prompt now contains other people's conversations. With a `;` and a second statement, the same trick reaches `DROP TABLE`. This is SQL injection, and it's been the top-ranked web vulnerability for two decades.

**Why `?` is immune.** The value never becomes part of the SQL text. SQLite parses the statement *first* — with the hole still in it — and produces a compiled plan where "compare this column against a value" is already fixed as the structure. Then the value is bound into that slot as data. A quote in the data is just a quote character; there's no parser left to confuse. The string `x' OR '1'='1` becomes a search for a thread literally named `x' OR '1'='1`, which matches nothing.

Structure comes from your code, values come from the tuple, and the two never mix.

A few practical notes:

- **The trailing comma matters.** `(THREAD_ID,)` is a one-element tuple; `(THREAD_ID)` is just a parenthesized string, and `execute` would raise an error about parameter count. Easy to trip on.
- **Placeholders are for values only.** You can't write `SELECT * FROM ?` — table and column names are structure, not data.
- **There's a named form too:** `WHERE thread_id = :tid` with `{"tid": THREAD_ID}`. Same protection, more readable when there are many parameters.

In this codebase `THREAD_ID` is a hardcoded constant, so nothing dangerous can reach it today. Using `?` anyway is the habit that matters — the day a thread id starts coming from a request header, the code is already correct.

|---|---|---|---|
| R1 baseline | 19 | 206 | 8,943 ms |

| R2 step 2 — last session | 350 | 35 | **5,537 ms** |
| R2 step 3 — weather | 397 | 329 | 19,166 ms |

Now look at step 2. It carried **the second-largest prompt of the whole session** — 350 input tokens, 18× the baseline — and it was the **fastest run we've made**. If input size drove latency, that row is impossible.

Sort by output instead and the pattern snaps into focus: 35 out → 5.5s, 206 out → 8.9s, 235 out → 15.8s, 329 out → 19.2s. Monotonic.

**Why: prefill is parallel, decode is sequential.**

Serving a request has two stages. First **prefill** — the model processes your entire input prompt. Every token is available at once, so this runs as a few large matrix operations across the whole sequence in parallel on the GPU. Adding 300 input tokens adds a slice to an already-parallel computation. Cheap in wall-clock.

Then **decode** — generating the reply. This is inherently one-token-at-a-time: the model can't produce token 50 until token 49 exists, because token 49 is part of the input to producing token 50. Each token is a full forward pass through the network. There is no parallelizing it.

So input tokens are *processed*; output tokens are *manufactured, in sequence*. Latency tracks the second.

**The reasoning-token wrinkle.** Step 2 still took 5.5 seconds for 35 visible tokens — 158 ms per token, far above the others. Remember what we found in the Round-1 detour: `reasoning_tokens=320` on a call whose visible reply was 185 tokens. Those hidden tokens are decoded one at a time exactly like visible ones. Step 2 almost certainly spent most of its 5.5 seconds thinking and then answered tersely. The visible-token column understates decode work, unevenly, on every row.

**What this means for your trade-off, and it's the useful part:**

> **Input tokens cost money. Output tokens cost time.**

Your deterministic read inflates input by 21× — that lands almost entirely on the bill and barely on the clock. Which is why Round 2's failure axis is stated as *cost, visibly*, not *slowness*. If it had been latency, you'd have felt it and fixed it immediately; a bill you don't look at is the failure that survives.

Two honest caveats: these are single samples over a network with no repeats, so ±2 seconds of noise is unremarkable — the ordering is meaningful, the exact numbers less so. And prefill isn't literally free; at tens of thousands of input tokens it becomes visible as time-to-first-token. At 400, it's in the noise.
